Outcome_variable.evidence_source: Cross-sectional analyses (see Table 2) showed that after adjustment for covariates, women who reported perceived sex discrimination were significantly more likely to report a diagnosis of clinical depression (OR 3.16; 95% CI [2.10, 4.79], p - .001) and were more likely to rate their health as fair/poor (OR 1.89; 95% CI [1.47, 2.41], p - .001) than those who did not report perceived sex discrimination. They also had significantly greater levels of psychological distress (B 1.26, 95% CI [0.95, 1.56], p - .001), poorer mental functioning (B 5.39, 95% CI [6.33, 4.46], p - .001), and lower life satisfaction (B 0.52, 95% CI [0.69, 0.36], p -.001). ... Possible scores on psychological distress, measured with the General Health Questionnaire, range from 0 to 12; possible scores on mental functioning, measured with the 12-Item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-12), range from 0 to 100; and possible life satisfaction scores scale range from 0 to 7.

sample_type.evidence_source: The paper describes a sample of 'women' but does not specify a nationally-representative sampling frame, clinical recruitment, or university student population. It is a general sample of women.

ethnicity.evidence_source: Table 1, Ethnicity section: 'No perceived sex discrimination' group (n = 2,380): White 16.3%, South Asian 40.2%, Black 24.9%, Other 18.6%. 'Perceived sex discrimination' group (n = 576): White 23.8%, South Asian 24.8%, Black 24.5%, Other 26.9%. No single ethnic group constitutes 70% or more of the sample.

lag.evidence_source: In prospective analyses (see Table 2) women who reported perceived sex discrimination had greater levels of psychological distress 4 years later than women who did not report perceived sex discrimination, independent of covariates (B 0.66, 95% CI [0.07, 1.24], p .029).
